claim: An estimated 23% of the world's population is latently infected with Mtb.
source: The World Health Organization reports that an estimated 23% of the world's population is latently infected with Mtb (https://www.who.int/tb/publications/global_report/en/).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO report

claim: Latent TB infections progress to active disease in 5–15% of cases.
source: Although asymptomatic and non-contagious, latent infections progress to active disease in 5–15% of cases, causing clinical symptoms and allowing for disease transmission (Pai et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pai et al., 2016

claim: The time before active disease develops following exposure to Mtb ranges from a few months to two years.
source: The time before active disease develops following exposure to Mtb, ranges from a few months to two years (Behr et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Behr et al., 2018

claim: In regions with minimal TB transmission, Mtb can persist in individuals for decades before causing active disease.
source: And, in regions with minimal TB transmission, Mtb can persist in individuals for decades before causing active disease (Behr et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Behr et al., 2018

claim: PerM is an integral membrane protein with 10 transmembrane helices.
source: We have previously reported that PerM, an integral membrane protein with 10 transmembrane helices is essential for Mtb persistence in the mouse model of infection.
evidence: Supported by previous report from the authors

claim: PerM is essential for Mtb persistence in the mouse model of infection.
source: We have previously reported that PerM, an integral membrane protein with 10 transmembrane helices is essential for Mtb persistence in the mouse model of infection.
evidence: Supported by previous report from the authors

claim: Disruption of perM by transposon insertion led to a minor growth defect in the acute phase of mouse infection.
source: Disruption of perM (rv0955) by transposon insertion led to a minor growth defect in the acute phase of mouse infection, but a strong attenuation in the chronic phase (Goodsmith et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goodsmith et al., 2015

claim: Disruption of perM by transposon insertion led to a strong attenuation in the chronic phase of mouse infection.
source: Disruption of perM (rv0955) by transposon insertion led to a minor growth defect in the acute phase of mouse infection, but a strong attenuation in the chronic phase (Goodsmith et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goodsmith et al., 2015

claim: The apparent static, non-replicating population that persists in chronically infected mice consists of a mixture of heterogeneous populations of replicating, non-replicating but alive, and dead bacteria.
source: In fact, the apparent static, non-replicating population that persists in chronically infected mice consists of a mixture of heterogeneous populations of replicating, non-replicating but alive, and dead bacteria (Gill et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gill et al., 2009

claim: Mtb replicates during the chronic phase of mouse infection, although at a much slower rate than in the acute phase.
source: Using a 'replication clock', a plasmid-based reporter of bacterial replication, Gill et al. showed that Mtb replicates during the chronic phase of mouse infection, although at a much slower rate than in the acute phase.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gill et al. work

claim: PerM is a mycobacterial divisome component.
source: Here, we demonstrate that PerM is a mycobacterial divisome component and facilitates cell division by stabilizing FtsB, a conserved divisome protein known to be essential for the initiation of septation (Buddelmeijer et al., 2002; Levin and Losick, 1994; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Demonstrated in this study through multiple experiments including immunoprecipitation and microscopy

claim: PerM facilitates cell division by stabilizing FtsB.
source: Here, we demonstrate that PerM is a mycobacterial divisome component and facilitates cell division by stabilizing FtsB, a conserved divisome protein known to be essential for the initiation of septation (Buddelmeijer et al., 2002; Levin and Losick, 1994; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Demonstrated in this study through protein stability assays and complementation experiments

claim: FtsB is a conserved divisome protein known to be essential for the initiation of septation.
source: Here, we demonstrate that PerM is a mycobacterial divisome component and facilitates cell division by stabilizing FtsB, a conserved divisome protein known to be essential for the initiation of septation (Buddelmeijer et al., 2002; Levin and Losick, 1994; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buddelmeijer et al., 2002; Levin and Losick, 1994; Wu et al., 2018

claim: PerM is dispensable during the acute phase of mouse infection.
source: We document that although PerM is dispensable during the acute phase of mouse infection, it is required for Mtb cell division during chronic mouse infection and in host-relevant stress conditions, during which maintaining an optimal FtsB level becomes crucial.
evidence: Demonstrated in this study through mouse infection experiments showing similar growth rates of WT and ΔperM during acute phase

claim: PerM is required for Mtb cell division during chronic mouse infection.
source: We document that although PerM is dispensable during the acute phase of mouse infection, it is required for Mtb cell division during chronic mouse infection and in host-relevant stress conditions, during which maintaining an optimal FtsB level becomes crucial.
evidence: Demonstrated in this study through replication clock experiments and cell length measurements

claim: PerM is required for Mtb cell division in host-relevant stress conditions.
source: We document that although PerM is dispensable during the acute phase of mouse infection, it is required for Mtb cell division during chronic mouse infection and in host-relevant stress conditions, during which maintaining an optimal FtsB level becomes crucial.
evidence: Demonstrated in this study through growth experiments at low pH and low iron conditions

claim: Maintaining an optimal FtsB level becomes crucial during chronic infection and host-relevant stress conditions.
source: We document that although PerM is dispensable during the acute phase of mouse infection, it is required for Mtb cell division during chronic mouse infection and in host-relevant stress conditions, during which maintaining an optimal FtsB level becomes crucial.
evidence: Inferred from complementation experiments showing FtsB overexpression rescues ΔperM phenotypes

claim: PerM represents the first reported bacterial divisome component that is conditionally essential for cell division at different stages of mouse infection.
source: To our knowledge, PerM represents the first reported bacterial divisome component that is conditionally essential for cell division at different stages of mouse infection.
evidence: Based on authors' knowledge of the literature and their experimental findings

claim: WT and ΔperM replicated at a similar rate in standard in vitro growth conditions.
source: Measurements of growth and plasmid loss showed that the two strains replicated at a similar rate in standard in vitro growth conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by growth curves and plasmid loss measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: During the initial two weeks after aerosol infection, WT and ΔperM grew logarithmically in mouse lungs.
source: During the initial two weeks after aerosol infection with approximately 1000 CFU, WT and ΔperM grew logarithmically in mouse lungs (Figure 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A with bacterial titers increasing exponentially

claim: The rate of plasmid loss was similar between WT and ΔperM during the first two weeks of infection.
source: The rate of plasmid loss was similar between WT and ΔperM (Figure 1B), resulting in a calculated doubling time of around 20 hr for both strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B with similar plasmid loss curves

claim: The calculated doubling time during the first two weeks of infection was around 20 hr for both WT and ΔperM strains.
source: The rate of plasmid loss was similar between WT and ΔperM (Figure 1B), resulting in a calculated doubling time of around 20 hr for both strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Calculated from plasmid loss data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: From 2 to 12 weeks post infection, WT Mtb persisted with stable bacterial titers.
source: From 2 to 12 weeks post infection, WT Mtb persisted with stable bacterial titers, while ΔperM titers decreased (Figure 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A with WT CFU remaining constant

claim: From 2 to 12 weeks post infection, ΔperM titers decreased.
source: From 2 to 12 weeks post infection, WT Mtb persisted with stable bacterial titers, while ΔperM titers decreased (Figure 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A with ΔperM CFU declining over time

claim: Plasmid loss was significantly slower in ΔperM than in WT during weeks 2-12 post infection.
source: Both strains lost the 'replication clock' plasmid more slowly than during the acute phase of infection, but plasmid loss was significantly slower in ΔperM than in WT (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance indicated

claim: The calculated doubling time of ΔperM during weeks 2-12 was 280 ± 61 hr.
source: The calculated doubling time of ΔperM was 280 ± 61 hr, more than twice the doubling time of WT, which was 111 ± 8 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Calculated from replication clock data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: The calculated doubling time of WT during weeks 2-12 was 111 ± 8 hr.
source: The calculated doubling time of ΔperM was 280 ± 61 hr, more than twice the doubling time of WT, which was 111 ± 8 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Calculated from replication clock data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: The cell replication rate of ΔperM was significantly lower than that of WT during weeks 2-12.
source: Consistently, the cell replication rate of ΔperM was significantly lower than that of WT while death rates were comparable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B with statistical analysis

claim: Death rates were comparable between WT and ΔperM during weeks 2-12.
source: Consistently, the cell replication rate of ΔperM was significantly lower than that of WT while death rates were comparable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: The cumulative bacterial burden of WT increased steadily during weeks 2–12.
source: We found that the CBB of WT increased steadily during weeks 2–12.
evidence: Calculated from replication and death rate data

claim: The cumulative bacterial burden of ΔperM increased only slightly during weeks 2-12.
source: In marked contrast, the CBB of ΔperM increased only slightly during the same time interval (Figure 1C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C

claim: The failure of ΔperM to persist in the chronic phase of mouse infection can be attributed to a cell replication defect.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that the failure of ΔperM to persist in the chronic phase of mouse infection can be attributed to a cell replication defect.
evidence: Inferred from replication clock data showing reduced replication rate but similar death rate

claim: At week two, WT and ΔperM had comparable median cell lengths in infected lung sections.
source: At week two, WT and ΔperM had comparable median cell lengths (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with cell length measurements

claim: At week three, ΔperM cells were significantly longer than WT cells in infected lung sections.
source: At week three, ΔperM cells were significantly longer than WT cells and this difference in cell length remained at weeks four and five.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance

claim: The observed cell replication defect is associated with impaired cell division during the chronic phase of mouse infection.
source: These measurements strongly suggest that the observed cell replication defect is associated with impaired cell division during the chronic phase of mouse infection.
evidence: Inferred from cell elongation phenotype which indicates failure to complete cell division

claim: MSMEG_5517 (PerMmsm) shares 73% identity with PerM from Mtb.
source: To explore how PerM facilitates cell division, we studied its homolog in M. smegmatis, a non-pathogenic mycobacterium; MSMEG_5517 (PerMmsm) shares 73% identity with PerM from Mtb.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison

claim: perMmsm is essential for growth of M. smegmatis.
source: Unexpectedly, we failed to isolate a perMmsm deletion mutant, which suggested that perMmsm is essential for growth of M. smegmatis.
evidence: Inferred from inability to isolate deletion mutant

claim: PerM depletion was bacteriostatic over the course of the experiment in M. smegmatis.
source: The number of viable cells remained constant in the PerM-depleted population, indicating that PerM depletion was bacteriostatic over the course of the experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D with CFU remaining constant

claim: PerM depletion resulted in an increase of median cell length from 4.46 µm to 11.1 µm in M. smegmatis.
source: PerM depletion resulted in an increase of median cell length from 4.46 µm to 11.1 µm in M. smegmatis (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A,B with cell length measurements

claim: The majority of elongated PerM-depleted cells contained either none or only one septum.
source: Additionally, peptidoglycan labeling with the fluorescent D-alanine analog HCC‐amino‐D‐alanine (HADA) revealed that the elongated cells formed filaments, with the majority containing either none or only one septum (Figure 2A,C) (Kuru et al., 2012; Kuru et al., 2015).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A,C with HADA labeling and quantification

claim: PerM depletion did not affect DNA segregation in M. smegmatis.
source: DNA staining with SYTO 13 revealed separated nucleoids spanning the entire length of each bacterium, suggesting that PerM depletion did not affect DNA segregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with DNA staining showing separated nucleoids

claim: PerM is involved in septation in M. smegmatis.
source: The phenotypes associated with PerM depletion in M. smegmatis demonstrate that PerM is involved in septation.
evidence: Inferred from cell elongation and reduced septum formation upon PerM depletion

claim: Ectopic expression of FtsBmtb or FtsBmsm rescued the growth defect caused by PerM depletion in M. smegmatis.
source: FtsBmtb is 72% identical to FtsBmsm, and ectopic expression of either protein from a multicopy plasmid rescued the growth defect caused by PerM depletion in M. smegmatis (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A with growth on atc-containing plates

claim: Ectopically-expressed FtsBmtb or FtsBmsm reversed the cell elongation phenotype in PerM-depleted M. smegmatis.
source: Furthermore, ectopically-expressed FtsBmtb or FtsBmsm reversed the cell elongation phenotype as did complementation with perMmtb or perMmsm (Figure 4B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B with cell length measurements

claim: PerM likely acts on FtsB to facilitate septum formation in M. smegmatis.
source: Therefore, PerM likely acts on FtsB to facilitate septum formation in M. smegmatis.
evidence: Inferred from FtsB complementation of PerM depletion phenotype

claim: FtsBmtb and FtsBmsm appear to be functionally conserved.
source: Moreover, FtsBmtb and FtsBmsm appear to be functionally conserved.
evidence: Inferred from both proteins rescuing PerM depletion phenotype

claim: Mtb lacking PerM elongated in response to Mg2+ limitation.
source: As we reported previously (Goodsmith et al., 2015), PerM is required for cell replication and survival of Mtb in media with reduced magnesium (Mg2+) and Mtb lacking PerM elongated in response to Mg2+ limitation (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C,D with growth curves and cell length measurements

claim: Both the growth and elongation phenotypes of ΔperM in low Mg2+ were rescued by ectopic expression of FtsB.
source: Both the growth and elongation phenotypes were, to a large extent, rescued by ectopic expression of FtsB, indicating that PerM likely functions via FtsB in Mtb as well.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C,D with complementation experiments

claim: PerM likely functions via FtsB in Mtb.
source: Both the growth and elongation phenotypes were, to a large extent, rescued by ectopic expression of FtsB, indicating that PerM likely functions via FtsB in Mtb as well.
evidence: Inferred from FtsB complementation of ΔperM phenotypes

claim: PerMmtb co-immunoprecipitated with FtsBmtb.
source: PerMmtb co-immunoprecipitated with FtsBmtb, suggesting that the two proteins are part of the same complex.
evidence: Shown by mass spectrometry analysis of FtsB immunoprecipitation (Table 1)

claim: PerM and FtsB are part of the same complex.
source: PerMmtb co-immunoprecipitated with FtsBmtb, suggesting that the two proteins are part of the same complex.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data

claim: FtsB interacts with FtsQ in Mtb.
source: The mass spectrometry data also revealed that FtsB interacts with FtsQ in Mtb (Table 1).
evidence: Shown in Table 1 from mass spectrometry data

claim: FtsQmtb has been shown to be a septal-localizing integral membrane protein that modulates cell division.
source: Similar to its homologs in E. coli and B. subtilis, FtsQmtb has been shown to be a septal-localizing integral membrane protein that modulates cell division (Buddelmeijer and Beckwith, 2004; Jain et al., 2018; Katis et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buddelmeijer and Beckwith, 2004; Jain et al., 2018; Katis et al., 2000

claim: FtsB, FtsL and FtsQ form a complex in E. coli.
source: FtsB, FtsL and FtsQ form a complex in E. coli (Buddelmeijer and Beckwith, 2004; Kureisaite-Ciziene et al., 2018), and here we provide evidence that the interaction between FtsB and FtsQ is conserved in mycobacteria.
evidence: Supported by citations to Buddelmeijer and Beckwith, 2004; Kureisaite-Ciziene et al., 2018

claim: The interaction between FtsB and FtsQ is conserved in mycobacteria.
source: FtsB, FtsL and FtsQ form a complex in E. coli (Buddelmeijer and Beckwith, 2004; Kureisaite-Ciziene et al., 2018), and here we provide evidence that the interaction between FtsB and FtsQ is conserved in mycobacteria.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data in this study

claim: FtsB localized to the mid-cell ahead of PerM during the cell cycle.
source: Time-lapse microscopy showed that FtsB localized to the mid-cell ahead of PerM (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A with time-lapse microscopy

claim: PerM localized to the same site approximately 15 min after FtsB.
source: PerM localized to the same site approximately 15 min later with both proteins present at the mid-cell prior to septum constriction.
evidence: Shown in time-lapse microscopy data

claim: FtsB signals started to increase at ~30% and peaked at ~50% of the cell cycle.
source: We quantified the fluorescence intensities at the mid-cell and observed that the FtsB signals started to increase at ~30% and peaked at ~50% of the cell cycle, whereas the PerM signals increased at ~40% and stabilized by ~50% of the cell cycle (Figure 5B), confirming that FtsB precedes PerM at the division site.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B with fluorescence intensity measurements

claim: PerM signals increased at ~40% and stabilized by ~50% of the cell cycle.
source: We quantified the fluorescence intensities at the mid-cell and observed that the FtsB signals started to increase at ~30% and peaked at ~50% of the cell cycle, whereas the PerM signals increased at ~40% and stabilized by ~50% of the cell cycle (Figure 5B), confirming that FtsB precedes PerM at the division site.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B with fluorescence intensity measurements

claim: The localization of FtsB to mid-cell does not depend on the presence of PerM.
source: In addition, in M. smegmatis lacking PerM but ectopically expressing a second copy of FtsB, FtsB also localized to the septum (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B). This suggests that the localization of FtsB to mid-cell does not depend on the presence of PerM.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B with microscopy of ΔperM expressing FtsB

claim: FtsB protein levels were markedly reduced in MtbΔperM relative to WT or the complemented mutant.
source: FtsB protein levels were markedly reduced in MtbΔperM relative to WT or the complemented mutant, despite similar ftsB mRNA levels (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C,D with western blot and qPCR data

claim: ftsB mRNA levels were similar between WT, ΔperM, and complemented mutant.
source: FtsB protein levels were markedly reduced in MtbΔperM relative to WT or the complemented mutant, despite similar ftsB mRNA levels (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D with qPCR data

claim: In both WT Mtb and the complemented mutant, FtsB amounts were stable over 96 hr after blocking protein synthesis.
source: In both WT Mtb and the complemented mutant, FtsB amounts were stable over 96 hr (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5E with western blot after chloramphenicol treatment

claim: FtsB abundance decreased over time in ΔperM after blocking protein synthesis.
source: In contrast, FtsB abundance decreased over time in ΔperM.
evidence: Shown in protein stability assay with chloramphenicol

claim: PerM stabilizes FtsB.
source: These results demonstrate that PerM stabilizes FtsB.
evidence: Demonstrated by protein stability assays showing FtsB degradation in absence of PerM

claim: MtbΔperM was specifically attenuated during the chronic phase of mouse infection following the onset of adaptive immunity.
source: MtbΔperM was specifically attenuated during the chronic phase of mouse infection following the onset of adaptive immunity when T-cell derived IFN-γ activates macrophages to control Mtb (Flynn et al., 1993).
evidence: Shown in mouse infection experiments and supported by citation to Flynn et al., 1993

claim: An Mtb perM transposon mutant survived host-relevant stresses similarly to WT in vitro.
source: We reported previously that an Mtb perM transposon mutant survived these stresses similarly to WT in vitro (Goodsmith et al., 2015), consistent with our finding that the death rates of ΔperM and WT were similar during the chronic phase of mouse infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goodsmith et al., 2015 and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: ΔperM exhibited a growth defect at pH 5.5.
source: In contrast to its near normal growth at pH 7, ΔperM exhibited a growth defect and elongated cell morphology at pH 5.5 (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A–C with growth curves and cell length measurements

claim: ΔperM exhibited elongated cell morphology at pH 5.5.
source: In contrast to its near normal growth at pH 7, ΔperM exhibited a growth defect and elongated cell morphology at pH 5.5 (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6C with cell length measurements

claim: Ectopically-expressed FtsB reversed the growth defect and cell elongation phenotype of ΔperM at pH 5.5.
source: Ectopically-expressed FtsB reversed the growth defect and cell elongation phenotype, suggesting that both were caused by insufficient amounts of FtsB.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A–C with complementation experiments

claim: FtsB levels were similar at pH 7 and pH 5.5.
source: Notably, FtsB levels were similar at pH 7 and pH 5.5, suggesting an increased demand for FtsB during growth at low pH (Figure 6D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6D with western blot

claim: There is an increased demand for FtsB during growth at low pH.
source: Notably, FtsB levels were similar at pH 7 and pH 5.5, suggesting an increased demand for FtsB during growth at low pH (Figure 6D).
evidence: Inferred from similar FtsB levels but requirement for PerM at low pH

claim: Growth in iron-depleted medium resulted in phenotypic changes similar to those observed at low pH.
source: Growth in iron-depleted medium resulted in phenotypic changes similar to those observed at low pH, and these could also be reversed by ectopic FtsB expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: In host-relevant stress conditions, PerM is required to maintain FtsB at levels that are sufficient for growth and cell division.
source: Therefore, in host-relevant stress conditions, PerM is required to maintain FtsB at levels that are sufficient for growth and cell division.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing PerM requirement and FtsB complementation under stress conditions

claim: Ectopic FtsB expression rescued the persistence defect of ΔperM in mice.
source: To extend these findings to the in vivo environment, we infected mice with ΔperM::ftsBmtb and found that ectopic FtsB expression rescued the persistence defect of ΔperM (Figure 6E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6E with mouse infection data

claim: PerM-mediated FtsB stabilization is required for growth and cell division in vivo, specifically in the chronic phase of infection.
source: Thus, PerM-mediated FtsB stabilization is required for growth and cell division in vivo, specifically in the chronic phase of infection.
evidence: Inferred from FtsB complementation rescuing ΔperM persistence defect

claim: Mtb cell division during the chronic phase of mouse infection depends on specific divisome components that differ from those required during the acute phase of infection.
source: Our results additionally highlight that Mtb cell division during the chronic phase of mouse infection depends on specific divisome components that differ from those required during the acute phase of infection.
evidence: Inferred from PerM being dispensable in acute phase but required in chronic phase

claim: Subclinical persistent infections caused by actively-growing bacteria have been described for multiple bacterial pathogens.
source: Subclinical persistent infections caused by actively-growing bacteria have been described for multiple bacterial pathogens (Certain et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Certain et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2017

claim: In individuals with latent TB infection, bacterial populations are heterogeneous, exhibit differences in metabolic state and susceptibility to antibiotics, and are likely to include actively-replicating subpopulations.
source: In individuals with latent TB infection, bacterial populations are heterogeneous, exhibit differences in metabolic state and susceptibility to antibiotics, and are likely to include actively-replicating subpopulations (Aldridge et al., 2012; Cadena et al., 2017; Esmail et al., 2016; Malherbe et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aldridge et al., 2012; Cadena et al., 2017; Esmail et al., 2016; Malherbe et al., 2016

claim: In E. coli, FtsB is associated with two other bitopic membrane proteins, FtsQ and FtsL, and promotes septation and cell constriction.
source: In E. coli, FtsB is associated with two other bitopic membrane proteins, FtsQ and FtsL, and promotes septation and cell constriction (Buddelmeijer and Beckwith, 2004; Glas et al., 2015), (Goehring and Beckwith, 2005; Liu et al., 2015; Tsang and Bernhardt, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Mycobacterial FtsQ, FtsL and FtsB are structurally conserved and functionally similar to their E. coli homologs.
source: Mycobacterial FtsQ, FtsL and FtsB are structurally conserved and functionally similar to their E. coli homologs (Jain et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018); however, regulation of FtsB differs between the two species.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jain et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018

claim: In E. coli, the stability of FtsB depends on FtsL and vice versa.
source: In E. coli, the stability of FtsB depends on FtsL and vice versa (Gonzalez and Beckwith, 2009), while we found that PerM is required to stabilize FtsB in Mtb; FtsL alone does not protect FtsB from degradation in the absence of PerM.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez and Beckwith, 2009

claim: FtsL alone does not protect FtsB from degradation in the absence of PerM in Mtb.
source: In E. coli, the stability of FtsB depends on FtsL and vice versa (Gonzalez and Beckwith, 2009), while we found that PerM is required to stabilize FtsB in Mtb; FtsL alone does not protect FtsB from degradation in the absence of PerM.
evidence: Demonstrated by FtsB degradation in ΔperM despite presence of FtsL

claim: PerM is highly conserved among mycobacteria and other actinobacteria but has no homologs outside of this group.
source: PerM is highly conserved among mycobacteria and other actinobacteria but has no homologs outside of this group, implying its function may be specific to actinobacteria.
evidence: Based on sequence homology searches

claim: PerM's function may be specific to actinobacteria.
source: PerM is highly conserved among mycobacteria and other actinobacteria but has no homologs outside of this group, implying its function may be specific to actinobacteria.
evidence: Inferred from lack of homologs outside actinobacteria

claim: PerM encoded by Mtb and M. smegmatis are conserved in function.
source: Within mycobacteria, we have shown that PerM encoded by Mtb and M. smegmatis are conserved in function (Figure 4B), but the two proteins differ in essentiality for growth under standard experimental conditions.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B with complementation experiments

claim: PerM from Mtb and M. smegmatis differ in essentiality for growth under standard experimental conditions.
source: Within mycobacteria, we have shown that PerM encoded by Mtb and M. smegmatis are conserved in function (Figure 4B), but the two proteins differ in essentiality for growth under standard experimental conditions.
evidence: Demonstrated by ability to delete perM in Mtb but not in M. smegmatis

claim: PerM may protect FtsB from recognition or access by an unidentified protease.
source: Nonetheless, PerM may protect FtsB from recognition or access by an unidentified protease.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on FtsB degradation in absence of PerM

claim: PerM may stabilize FtsB and possibly the FtsQLB complex by facilitating protein-protein interactions within the divisome.
source: Alternatively, PerM may stabilize FtsB and possibly the FtsQLB complex (Wu et al., 2018) by facilitating protein-protein interactions within the divisome.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on PerM-FtsB interaction data

claim: In B. subtilis, FtsL degradation by RasP has been proposed to occur after the cell cycle has been completed and the divisome disassembled.
source: In B. subtilis, FtsL degradation by RasP has been proposed to occur after the cell cycle has been completed and the divisome disassembled, thus preventing reassembly of the divisome and subsequent cell division at the wrong time (Wadenpohl and Bramkamp, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wadenpohl and Bramkamp, 2010

claim: In E. coli, the concentration of FtsZ has been shown to oscillate during the cell cycle in slow growth conditions.
source: In E. coli, the concentration of FtsZ has been shown to oscillate during the cell cycle in slow growth conditions and FtsZ is degraded by the ClpXP protease at the end of the cell cycle (Männik et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Männik et al., 2018

claim: FtsZ is degraded by the ClpXP protease at the end of the cell cycle in E. coli.
source: In E. coli, the concentration of FtsZ has been shown to oscillate during the cell cycle in slow growth conditions and FtsZ is degraded by the ClpXP protease at the end of the cell cycle (Männik et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Männik et al., 2018

claim: The amplitude of FtsZ oscillation increased in conditions where growth is slowed in E. coli.
source: Further, the amplitude of FtsZ oscillation increased in conditions where growth is slowed, indicating that growth conditions may impact the regulation of cell division.
evidence: Based on cited work on FtsZ oscillation

claim: The expression of an unstable FtsB along with its stabilizer PerM may allow for fine-tuning of FtsB levels during the cell cycle in Mtb.
source: In Mtb, the expression of an unstable FtsB along with its stabilizer PerM may allow for fine-tuning of FtsB levels during the cell cycle, which could be important in adaptation to the host environment.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on FtsB instability and PerM stabilization

claim: Either FtsB activity is altered under stress conditions or the divisome formed in Mtb under stress conditions differs from the standard log-phase divisome, displaying an increased demand for FtsB.
source: This observation indicates that either FtsB activity is altered under stress conditions or that the divisome formed in Mtb under stress conditions differs from the standard log-phase divisome, displaying an increased demand for FtsB.
evidence: Inferred from similar FtsB levels but different requirements under stress

claim: MarP interacts more strongly with the peptidoglycan hydrolase RipA in acidic pH, resulting in RipA activation.
source: For example, MarP, a periplasmic protease, interacts more strongly with the peptidoglycan hydrolase RipA in acidic pH, resulting in RipA activation (Botella et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Botella et al., 2017a

claim: FtsZ requires interaction with FipA for mid-cell localization and Z-ring formation in M. smegmatis during oxidative stress, but not in normal growth conditions.
source: In addition, FtsZ requires interaction with FipA for mid-cell localization and Z-ring formation in M. smegmatis during oxidative stress, but not in normal growth conditions (Sureka et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sureka et al., 2010

claim: Z-ring formation has been shown to be compromised in intracellular Mtb, likely due to altered FtsZ stability or activity in stresses imposed by the intracellular environment.
source: Z-ring formation has also been shown to be compromised in intracellular Mtb, likely due to altered FtsZ stability or activity in stresses imposed by the intracellular environment (Chauhan et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chauhan et al., 2006

claim: The environmental stimuli regulating cell division proteins are often transduced by protein kinases.
source: The environmental stimuli regulating cell division proteins are often transduced by protein kinases (Molle and Kremer, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Molle and Kremer, 2010

claim: The co-immunoprecipitation experiment revealed interaction of FtsB with PknH, a Ser/Thr protein kinase involved in regulation of cell division.
source: In addition to PerM and FtsQ, our co-immunoprecipitation experiment revealed interaction of FtsB with PknH, a Ser/Thr protein kinase involved in regulation of cell division (Sharma et al., 2006; Zheng et al., 2007) (Table 1).
evidence: Shown in Table 1 and supported by citations to Sharma et al., 2006; Zheng et al., 2007

claim: The requirements for cell division differ in vitro between standard growth conditions and host-relevant stress conditions.
source: The cell division and in vivo persistence defects caused by inactivating PerM, a protein dispensable for bacterial replication in standard in vitro growth conditions, reveal that the requirements for cell division differ in vitro between standard growth conditions and host-relevant stress conditions, as well as in vivo between acute and chronic phases of mouse infection.
evidence: Demonstrated by PerM being dispensable in standard conditions but required under stress

claim: The requirements for cell division differ in vivo between acute and chronic phases of mouse infection.
source: The cell division and in vivo persistence defects caused by inactivating PerM, a protein dispensable for bacterial replication in standard in vitro growth conditions, reveal that the requirements for cell division differ in vitro between standard growth conditions and host-relevant stress conditions, as well as in vivo between acute and chronic phases of mouse infection.
evidence: Demonstrated by PerM being dispensable in acute phase but required in chronic phase

claim: Evidence for ongoing bacterial transcription and bacterial heterogeneity during latent TB infection support the hypothesis that sustained cell replication facilitates persistence of Mtb in humans.
source: Whether sustained cell replication also facilitates persistence of Mtb in humans is as yet unknown, but evidence for ongoing bacterial transcription and bacterial heterogeneity during latent TB infection support this hypothesis (Esmail et al., 2016; Malherbe et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Esmail et al., 2016; Malherbe et al., 2016

claim: After aerosol infection, Mtb replicates logarithmically in mouse lungs until the onset of adaptive immunity arrests replication, leading to a chronic infection that is contained but not eliminated.
source: After aerosol infection, Mtb replicates logarithmically in mouse lungs until the onset of adaptive immunity arrests replication, leading to a chronic infection that is contained but not eliminated.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mouse TB infection model

claim: Metabolic adaption and modulation of the cell envelope play key roles in Mtb's persistence.
source: Among those pathways, metabolic adaption and modulation of the cell envelope play key roles in Mtb's persistence (Ehrt et al., 2018; Glickman and Jacobs, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ehrt et al., 2018; Glickman and Jacobs, 2001

claim: In IFN-γ-activated macrophages, Mtb faces acidic pH, reactive oxygen and nitrogen intermediates and limited amounts of iron and other nutrients.
source: In IFN-γ-activated macrophages, Mtb faces acidic pH, reactive oxygen and nitrogen intermediates and limited amounts of iron and other nutrients (Ehrt and Schnappinger, 2009; Stallings and Glickman, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ehrt and Schnappinger, 2009; Stallings and Glickman, 2010

claim: The percentage of septa labeled with NADA alone declined after PerM depletion.
source: The percentage of septa labeled with NADA alone declined from 23.77% (no atc) to 14.62%, 12.56% and 15.92% after 1.5, 4 and 10 hr incubation with atc (Figure 3D), suggesting that PerM-depleted cells had an impaired ability to form new septa.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3D with quantification of NADA-labeled septa

claim: PerM-depleted cells had an impaired ability to form new septa.
source: The percentage of septa labeled with NADA alone declined from 23.77% (no atc) to 14.62%, 12.56% and 15.92% after 1.5, 4 and 10 hr incubation with atc (Figure 3D), suggesting that PerM-depleted cells had an impaired ability to form new septa.
evidence: Inferred from decreased proportion of newly formed septa

claim: The proportion of HADA-containing septa increased with time after PerM depletion.
source: In contrast, the proportion of HADA-containing septa increased with time, from 0.61% (no atc) to 1.14%, 5.34% and 8.48% after 1.5, 4 and 10 hr atc treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3E with quantification of HADA-labeled septa

claim: PerM depletion affects both septum formation and cell separation in M. smegmatis.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that PerM depletion affects both septum formation and cell separation in M. smegmatis, causing the bacteria to form filaments.
evidence: Inferred from sequential labeling experiments showing defects in both processes

claim: FtsBmtb is 72% identical to FtsBmsm.
source: FtsBmtb is 72% identical to FtsBmsm, and ectopic expression of either protein from a multicopy plasmid rescued the growth defect caused by PerM depletion in M. smegmatis (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison

claim: Survival of Mtb during chronic infection depends on a persistence divisome.
source: These data highlight the importance of sustained cell division for Mtb persistence, define condition-specific requirements for cell division and reveal that survival of Mtb during chronic infection depends on a persistence divisome.
evidence: Inferred from PerM being specifically required during chronic infection

claim: The FtsQLB complex is thought to drive septation by stimulating peptidoglycan synthesis by the peptidoglycan synthases FtsI and FtsW along with their associated proteins.
source: The FtsQLB complex is thought to drive septation by stimulating peptidoglycan synthesis by the peptidoglycan synthases FtsI and FtsW along with their associated proteins (Kureisaite-Ciziene et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2015; Taguchi et al., 2019; Tsang and Bernhardt, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Depletion of FtsQ, FtsL or FtsB in M. smegmatis resulted in morphological changes indicative of impaired septation.
source: Like in E. coli, depletion of FtsQ, FtsL or FtsB in M. smegmatis resulted in morphological changes indicative of impaired septation (Buddelmeijer et al., 2002; Carson et al., 1991; Guzman et al., 1992; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: In B. subtilis, the FtsB homolog DivIC interacts with FtsL, preventing proteolysis of FtsL by the intramembrane protease RasP.
source: A similar scenario has been observed in B. subtilis, the FtsB homolog DivIC interacts with FtsL, preventing proteolysis of FtsL by the intramembrane protease RasP (Wadenpohl and Bramkamp, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wadenpohl and Bramkamp, 2010
